Short-billed dowitchers (Limnodromus griseus) exhibit a life history finely tuned to their arctic and subarctic breeding grounds, where the brief summer window constrains reproductive timing. Eggs are deposited in a shallow nest cup lined with grasses, and incubation is shared by both parents. The incubation period, during which eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days]. Newly hatched chicks emerge weighing about 11.8 grams [Wwb = about 11.8 grams], a modest mass that reflects the semi-precocial developmental strategy of this species. At this initial size, the downy young are capable of leaving the nest within hours of hatching, though they remain dependent on adults for thermoregulation and foraged food items. This birth weight, while low in absolute terms, is consistent with the energetic constraints faced by shorebird chicks that must rapidly gain mass to fledge before the onset of the northern winter.

Under the thermal conditions typical of a parentally brooded chick, with body temperatures sustained around 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the fledgling stage is reached 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching]. At this point, the young dowitcher attains flight capability and begins to forage independently, although parental provisioning may continue for a brief period. The rapid progression from hatching to fledging in just three weeks is a critical adaptation for a species that must complete its full breeding cycle, including the rearing of a single brood, within the brief arctic summer. This developmental pace places considerable metabolic demand on the growing chick, which must nearly double its hatch weight several times over during this short interval. The male and female both contribute to feeding the brood, with adults transporting invertebrate prey from nearby mudflats and wetlands to the young.

Females of this species ultimately attain an adult body mass of 105 grams [Wwi = 105 grams], a size that positions them among the larger scolopacids within their genus. This ultimate wet weight for females is achieved through a period of rapid somatic growth following fledging, during which juveniles exploit abundant food resources on southerly staging grounds. The disparity between hatchling mass and adult mass underscores the substantial energetic investment required to bridge this tenfold difference. Body condition at the time of migration is a strong predictor of survival and future reproductive success, with heavier females generally demonstrating higher fecundity in subsequent seasons. Adult dowitchers maintain this mass through a diet dominated by aquatic invertebrates, including fly larvae, small mollusks, and annelids, which they extract from soft sediments using a distinctive probing foraging motion.

Sexual maturation in the Short-billed dowitcher is attained relatively early for a long-distance migratory shorebird. At a body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], which is the core temperature maintained by actively foraging adults, puberty is documented to occur 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching]. This rapid progression to reproductive potential reflects the selective pressure for individuals to breed as soon as possible upon reaching breeding grounds in their second calendar year, particularly given the short arctic window. However, despite reaching physiological sexual maturity within roughly two months of hatching, most individuals do not actually breed during their first return to the north. Instead, they typically delay their first successful breeding event until their second spring, when they have accumulated sufficient body reserves and have likely secured a territory and a mate.

The first successful brood from a Short-billed dowitcher is typically produced at an age of 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], coinciding with the species’ return to its arctic breeding grounds in the late spring of its second year at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This timing, measured under the sustained 41 °C [T = 41 °C] body temperature of an active adult, means that first-time breeders are approximately one year old when they lay their clutch. Females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], with each clutch containing a typical of 4 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing a typical of 4 eggs], a reproductive rate that results in a maximum output of 4 eggs per year. At this rate, and given that a single clutch is the norm, the annual reproductive output is modest. Longevity data indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of roughly 13.3 years [am = roughly 13.3 years] when active body temperature is near 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a figure that reflects the demographic profile of a small-bodied shorebird balancing migratory risk against multi-year breeding potential.
